Nuclear engineers design, operate, maintain, and analyze the safety of nuclear-energy systems. Their work includes reactor-physics and thermal-hydraulic calculations, fuel management, radiation protection, nuclear-safety assessment, and facility decommissioning, making this one of the most specialized engineering roles in the nuclear-energy value chain.

paragraphs: A typical day starts by reviewing overnight operating data for parameter fluctuations. The morning includes a meeting on a safety-analysis issue, and the afternoon involves simulation calculations and validation of design assumptions. On inspection days, engineers wear protective clothing in the plant. The evening brings report writing and approvals. In nuclear work, a qualified report matters more than a clever idea.

U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data show that about 15,400 nuclear engineers were employed in 2024. Employment is projected to fall to 15,300 by 2034, a net loss of about 100 jobs, with roughly 800 openings per year and a median annual wage of about $127,500 in 2026 (BLS OOH, 2026).

AI will not replace nuclear engineers, but it will change calculation work. Safety analyses that once took several days can now converge quickly with AI and supercomputing, while surrogate models assist parameter optimization previously guided by experience. Core responsibilities such as design decisions, safety reviews, and response to operational anomalies still require people. AI provides results, but only engineers bear responsibility for deciding whether to use them.
